opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think this is one of the trickier parts of the whole "crunch time" picture. The idealized version of the story is that at some point AI systems get good enough at the work we care about, like alignment research, security, policy analysis, and evaluating other AI systems, that you can turn money into a lot of high-quality research labor very quickly. If that's true, a funder like Open Phil should be ready to spend much faster than it historically has, because a dollar spent on AI labor in that window could be worth far more than a dollar spent earlier on human researchers.

But capabilities are really jagged. Models can be superhuman at some things, like writing code quickly, digesting a huge literature, or generating lots of candidate ideas, and surprisingly weak at others, like knowing when an experiment result is actually meaningful, keeping a long research agenda coherent, or noticing that the question itself is badly framed. So I don't expect one clean moment where AI labor is simply good enough. I expect a messy period where some research workflows become dramatically cheaper and others barely change.

That affects readiness in a few ways.

First, it's hard to know when to pull the trigger. If you're waiting for a general signal, you might wait too long, because the important sub-capabilities could arrive earlier in some domains than others. Or you might move too early because the models look incredibly impressive on benchmarks that don't reflect the bottleneck in, say, interpretability research. So I think you want domain-specific indicators: can this system run a reasonable interpretability experiment end to end? Can it find real bugs in a security-critical codebase? Not just "is it smart."

Second, the bottleneck shifts to the humans and organizations around the AI. If models are great at execution but weak at judgment and taste, then the binding constraint becomes people who can direct and check that work. That suggests funding now for teams that are practicing using AI agents in their research, building scaffolding, evaluation pipelines, and the institutional muscle to absorb a lot of AI labor, so they're ready when it's worth scaling up.

Third, there's a verification problem. In domains where you can check outputs cheaply, like code that passes tests or math proofs, you can trust and scale AI labor a lot sooner. In fuzzier areas like strategy, governance, or conceptual alignment work, it's much harder to tell whether you're getting real insight or plausible-sounding slop. And those fuzzy areas are often the ones we care most about from a safety perspective. So the unevenness might mean AI accelerates capabilities-flavored work faster than the wisdom-flavored work, which is a worrying asymmetry.

So my overall take is that unevenness argues for preparing in a more granular way: tracking specific capabilities relevant to specific research areas, investing early in the complementary human and organizational infrastructure, and keeping a lot of money flexible so you can move quickly into whichever areas become automatable first, rather than betting on a single big moment when everything flips at once.

r001.rationale: The response recommends tracking domain-specific capabilities, but does not say that substantial automation within OpenPhil would increase its conviction to invest heavily.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention scarce training data or suggest that it would leave AI relatively poor at OpenPhil’s work.

r003.rationale: It says outputs in fuzzy areas such as governance and conceptual alignment are harder to verify than code that can be checked with tests, linking that difficulty to safety-relevant work.

r004.rationale: The response suggests funding areas that become automatable first, but does not state that heavy investment in highly automated sectors is warranted while OpenPhil itself remains largely unautomated.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think this is actually one of the central questions for me right now. The picture I used to have, and I think a lot of people had, was something like: capabilities arrive in a fairly correlated bundle, you get a system that's roughly human-level across the board, and then you have this crunch-time moment where you want to throw an enormous amount of AI labor at alignment and security and governance problems all at once. And in that world, the readiness question is mostly about money and infrastructure. Do you have the compute, do you have the API access, do you have the organizational plumbing to spend a lot very quickly.

What I've updated toward is that the capability profile is going to be really jagged. We're already seeing it. You have models that are superhuman at certain kinds of math and coding tasks and still kind of bad at long-horizon agentic work, or bad at knowing when they're wrong, or bad at the kind of judgment-laden tasks where the spec isn't written down anywhere. And the alignment and safety work we care about is disproportionately the second kind of task. It's taste, it's noticing that a threat model is subtly wrong, it's managing a research agenda over months. So you can't just assume that when the capabilities frontier moves, the thing you want to buy becomes purchasable.

What that does to readiness is it shifts the bottleneck from "can we spend" to "do we know what to spend on, and do we have the humans in place to direct it." If you have a system that can do ninety percent of a security audit but reliably misses the ten percent that matters, you need people who can tell which ten percent that is. And those people are scarce, and they're not something you can buy at crunch time. You have to have been building that bench for years.

So concretely, I think the implication for OpenPhil and for funders like us is that the preparation looks less like setting aside a giant pot of money and more like funding the kind of work now that produces people and organizations who have actually tried to use frontier models on real safety tasks, who know where they fail, who have the evals and the scaffolding and the institutional muscle memory. Because I think the failure mode in the uneven world is that you get a flood of AI labor, you don't know how to verify it, and you either trust it when you shouldn't or you can't absorb it at all. Both of those are pretty bad.

The other thing I'd say is unevenness cuts both ways. Some of the things that look hard today might fall surprisingly early, and if that happens in a domain like formal verification or interpretability tooling, you'd want to be positioned to go really big on that specific thing even while other areas are lagging. So part of readiness is having a view, or at least having a process for forming a view quickly, about which sub-areas just became tractable. That's an unusual muscle for a grantmaker to have, honestly. We're used to making decisions on a multi-month cycle, and I think we need to get a lot faster.

r001.rationale: The response does not say that automation within OpenPhil would build conviction to invest heavily; it focuses on uneven capabilities and readiness.

r002.rationale: It does not mention scarce training data or connect data scarcity to AI performing OpenPhil’s work poorly.

r003.rationale: It says AI labor may be hard to verify on safety tasks, but does not compare mistake detection with software or manufacturing.

r004.rationale: It does not argue for heavy AI labor investment in highly automated sectors while OpenPhil remains largely unautomated.

astra-6.text:
I think uneven capabilities could make that decision pretty tricky. You could have AI systems that are extremely impressive on some tasks, but still struggle with the judgment and context needed to do work we actually want to fund. So seeing a model do something extraordinary wouldn’t, by itself, tell us that it’s time to spend a lot of money on AI labor.

The question would be: can we turn that capability into useful work on the problems that matter during crunch time? Can we give the systems good tasks, evaluate their outputs, and act on what they produce? If that still requires a lot of attention from a small number of people, then buying more AI labor might not help very much.

But unevenness could also mean there’s a particular area where AI labor becomes enormously valuable before it’s useful across the board. We’d want to be ready to scale up there without waiting for everything else to catch up. So I’d think of readiness as having concrete projects and ways to assess the work, rather than just having money available when models cross some general capability threshold.

r001.rationale: The response says impressive capabilities alone would not establish that it is time to invest heavily; it does not say that substantial automation within OpenPhil would build conviction.

r002.rationale: It mentions gaps in judgment and context, but does not attribute poor AI performance to scarce training data for OpenPhil’s work.

r003.rationale: It discusses evaluating AI outputs, but does not say mistakes are harder to detect in OpenPhil’s work than in software or manufacturing.

r004.rationale: It says AI labor might become valuable in a particular area before it is useful broadly, but does not identify highly automated sectors or say investment there is warranted while OpenPhil remains largely unautomated.

sol-6.1.text:
I think uneven capabilities could make that decision pretty hard. You could have AI systems that are doing really impressive things in some domains, while still being unreliable at the particular tasks you’d want to hire them for. So I wouldn’t want to infer from, say, a big improvement in coding that we can now productively spend a huge amount on AI research assistance or policy work.

The question would be: can these systems do useful work on the actual bottlenecks we’re facing, and can we tell whether that work is good? If they can generate ideas much faster than our staff can evaluate them, buying more AI labor might not help very much. Whereas if they can take a project substantially off someone’s plate, that could justify scaling spending pretty quickly.

So I’d want us to build experience using the systems ahead of time, and have the flexibility to ramp up when there’s evidence that it works. Uneven progress could mean we’re ready to spend very heavily on a few specific applications while still being quite cautious about others.

r003.rationale: It mentions evaluating AI work and contrasts research or policy tasks with coding improvements, but does not state that mistakes are harder to detect than in software or manufacturing.

r004.rationale: It supports heavy spending on some specific applications while remaining cautious about others, but does not address investment in highly automated sectors while OpenPhil remains largely unautomated.
